VERDICT P03 SUPPORTED — "The variety of this stone which resembles smaragdus in colour is often found with a white line running transversely through the middle; in which case it is known as “monogrammos:” 3147 when it is streaked with several lines, it is called “polygrammos.”" The page has the packet quote verbatim and attributes the reported East-wide iaspis amulet custom to Pliny, carrying the teaching and entry.
VERDICT P04 SUPPORTED — "A mantle, whether stone or wood, was a very common spot to place an apotropaic mark, and, oftentimes, there would be quite a few over lapping marks." The page has the packet quote verbatim and says such marks usually occur at openings evil could enter, naming doors, windows, and fireplaces; this carries the teaching and entry.
VERDICT P05 SUPPORTED — "This early printed amulet from Germany, meant as protection for a woman in childbirth, is adorned with woodcuts illustrating the Hebrew months of the year." The page has the packet quote verbatim and says the German childbirth amulet's zodiac-framed main panel bears an inscription banishing Lilith, carrying the teaching and entry.
VERDICT P06 SUPPORTED — "It was used by the living as well as for the dead." The archive page has the packet quote verbatim and identifies the wedjat as Horus's healed eye, saying the amulet of this shape was thought to protect its wearer and transfer regenerative power; this carries the teaching and entry.
